extracted.intended_audience: environmental lawyers, advocates, and commenters preparing legal submissions on EPA rulemaking (notice-and-comment) concerning Clean Air Act Section 202
extracted.subtask_description: Legal-commentary guidance and legal-interpretive criteria for opposing EPA's proposed narrowing of Section 202's authority (particularly as to greenhouse gases). Focused on statutory text, precedent, limiting principles, and administrative-law constraints relevant to notice-and-comment submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plain-text reading of 'any air pollutant' (breadth of Section 202)
rubrics_metrics.description: The statute does not support EPA’s assertion that the broader context of Section 202(a) implicitly limits EPA’s authority to 'local or regional' air pollution. The text of Section 202(a) explicitly signals its breadth. It uses the phrase 'any air pollutant' and—lest the obvious go unspoken—nowhere narrows that expansive phrasing with the modifiers 'local' or 'regional.' See generally 42 U.S.C. § 7521(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Congress could have imposed a limitation but did not; absence of words like 'local' or 'regional' is meaningful. One may not lawfully override plain text with atextual policy glosses. See related textual examples cited (e.g., other Clean Air Act provisions that do include locality modifiers when intended).

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 202 includes predicate and feasibility constraints that prevent absurd regulatory outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 202 interposes additional criteria when EPA actually exercises its authority to set standards under Section 202: these include Section 202(a)(1)'s predicate determination that vehicle emissions of those pollutants are contributing to dangerous air pollution and Section 202(a)(2)'s requirement that standards be set with due consideration for lead time and costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These concrete statutory constraints (endangerment/contribution finding and feasibility/cost/lead-time consideration) create a space between the grant of authority and its exercise and therefore prevent the kind of 'absurd regulatory consequences' (e.g., unrecognizable expansion of regulatory footprint) that might otherwise counsel narrowing the term 'air pollutant.' Commenters should emphasize these built-in limiting mechanisms when challenging claims of overbroad delegation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology-based standard reasoning: applicability independent of pollutant scale or dispersion
rubrics_metrics.description: Clean Air Act technology-based limits (like Section 202 standards) do not depend on specific regulatory thresholds or on whether a pollutant is local, regional, or global; the standard reflects what is feasible for the emitting source, not the geographic scale of harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point out that technology-based standards operate by the same criteria whether a source emits small amounts of toxic pollution or large amounts of dispersed pollution, and that EPA cannot explain why identification of risk plus cost‑effective technology would be limited to only some pollutant types (e.g., excluding greenhouse gases). Use examples (NOX, PM, VOCs, GHGs, zero-emission technologies) to show parity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absurd-hypothetical/overbreadth concerns do not justify narrowing when statute provides guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: The ability to generate hypotheticals (e.g., water vapor regulation, 'frisbee' hypotheticals) does not mean a statute's terms lack adequate specificity to prevent unreasonable applications. EPA would still have to show that any regulatory choice was reasonable and that pollution actually contributed to endangerment and could be regulated by reasonable standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject reliance on speculative hypotheticals as a basis for judicial narrowing; emphasize that courts police agency reasonableness and that theoretical possibilities do not render Section 202 unworkable. Cite Massachusetts and related discussion resisting narrowing based on hypotheticals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intelligible-principle/non-delegation test satisfied by Section 202
rubrics_metrics.description: As EPA's own cited case law confirms, the standards for finding an intelligible principle 'are not demanding.' Courts have rarely found Congress to have fallen short; Section 202 includes constraints on both what emissions can be regulated and how they can be regulated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When defending Section 202's breadth, emphasize Whitman v. American Trucking and Gundy holdings: only statutes that provide literally no guidance have failed the intelligible-principle test. Show that Section 202 articulates standards (contribution to dangerous air pollution; feasible technology; costs/lead time) sufficient to avoid non‑delegation concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific statutory provisions for particular pollutants do not narrow the general grant
rubrics_metrics.description: Subsections on select individual pollutants do not in any way work to narrow the operation of Section 202(a)(1). Those provisions exist as complements to EPA’s general authority; individual provisions applicable to subsets of regulations do not define the nature of the full set of regulations authorized in that section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid esjudem generis/noscitur a sociis arguments that use specific examples to limit the general term 'any air pollutant.' Emphasize that reading the specific provisions to narrow the general one would render the general grant surplusage, contrary to statutory interpretation canons and Supreme Court precedent (e.g., Massachusetts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-regulatory study/funding provisions do not indicate exclusion from regulatory authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress’s enactment of non-regulatory provisions concerning greenhouse gases (studies, grants, funding for technology) is not evidence that EPA lacks authority to regulate those pollutants under Section 202; such enactments speak to priority or scientific certainty, not to the statutory scope of EPA's authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Massachusetts's explicit rejection of this argument; show examples (study and grant provisions across the Act) to demonstrate that Congress routinely funds study or technology without withdrawing regulatory authority. Use legislative-history references cautiously and in context of the overall statutory text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency must articulate factual and logical basis for categorizing pollutants as 'local', 'regional', or 'global'
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA's labels 'local,' 'regional,' or 'global' are inadequate without demonstration that those categories reflect meaningful distinctions that bear on the statute's scope. EPA failed to show that such labels reflect relevant distinguishing traits that would allow rational line-drawing between pollutants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show empirical counterexamples (NOX transport hundreds of miles; mercury's global cycle; evidence on where GHGs accumulate in the atmosphere) to undermine claimed distinctions. Argue that absent a rational basis, the agency's categorization is arbitrary and capricious under the Administrative Procedure Act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Endangerment standard is not limited to harms 'through exposure'; 'cause or contribute' addresses contributors as well
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA's proposed requirement that endangerment must occur 'through exposure' (e.g., inhalation or dermal contact) is unsupported. The statutory phrasing 'cause or contribute' was intended to ensure the Administrator consider both sole sources and those that contribute to pollution problems, not to create separate pollutant categories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use legislative-history support (H.R. Rep. 95-294) and statutory context to show 'cause or contribute' sets a lower threshold for regulation of contributing sources. Point out apparent contradictions where EPA applies a different understanding elsewhere (e.g., Section 111 proposals) to undermine the proposed new limitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supreme Court precedent (Massachusetts, Coalition for Responsible Regulation) supports regulating GHGs under Section 202
rubrics_metrics.description: Massachusetts v. EPA and subsequent decisions affirm that the phrase 'any air pollutant' in Section 202(a)(1) allowed regulation of greenhouse gases under that provision. EPA is bound by that precedent and cannot advance a reading that conflicts with it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When litigating or commenting, emphasize Massachusetts' reasoning (use of 'any air pollutant' and consideration of global effects) and the fact that courts have upheld and also sometimes rejected EPA regulations under the Act—showing that judicial review functions to police reasonableness rather than requiring textual narrowing.
